headline: AI stocks meet voters, a smarter salt, and a noisier planet
teaser: Can voters slow the AI boom? Should governments change the salt in our food? And what is human noise costing wildlife?

articles.title: When Politics Meets the Algorithm: The Day AI Stocks Fell
articles.dek: Voters, not engineers, may decide how fast the AI boom can grow. Was Thursday's crash a warning or an overreaction?
paras: For much of the past four years, shares in companies building artificial intelligence have behaved as if gravity no longer applied to them. Chipmakers, cloud providers and data-centre developers soared as investors bet that demand for computing power would keep climbing for a decade. On Thursday, November 5, 2026, that confidence met an unexpected obstacle: an election. Two days after Democrats won majorities in both chambers of the US Congress, global stock markets fell sharply, led by a dramatic sell-off in technology shares.

The scale of the decline was striking. According to Reuters, the Nasdaq Composite, an index dominated by technology firms, dropped 5.5 percent, confirming a correction, which means a fall of at least 10 percent from its recent peak. The broader S&P 500 slid 4.4 percent, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged 12.2 percent, its steepest single-day drop since April 2025. Nvidia, the leading supplier of AI chips, lost roughly 9 percent of its value in a single session, and estimates of the total market value erased on Wall Street reached about $2.5 trillion. Asian and European markets fell as well, although US technology shares partially recovered on Friday.

What makes the episode puzzling is that markets had initially welcomed the result. On Wednesday, stocks rose, partly because the outcome was clear and quick, which removed a layer of uncertainty. By Thursday, however, investors had begun to read the details more closely. Several newly elected officials had campaigned on slowing or pausing the construction of data centres, the vast warehouses of servers that train and run AI systems. Across the country, voters decided on 45 ballot measures related to data centres and backed restrictions in most of them. In Texas, one of the busiest states for data-centre development, the governor-elect has promised a moratorium on new projects until lawmakers enact stronger protections. Analysts at the Swiss bank UBS estimated that construction pauses could put about 30 percent of the US data-centre capacity planned for 2028 at risk.

Why would voters object to buildings full of computers? The answer lies largely in their appetite for resources. The largest data centres can consume as much electricity as a small city, and in many regions residents have blamed such facilities for rising power bills, heavy water use and constant noise. For local communities, the benefits, such as construction jobs and tax revenue, can seem modest compared with the costs, which are spread across every household connected to the grid. The election, in this sense, turned an abstract technological boom into a concrete local question: who pays for the infrastructure of the future?

Not everyone interprets the sell-off as a turning point. Many analysts argue that long-term demand for chips and computing power remains intact, and that the political shock will produce, at most, a temporary slowdown rather than a reversal. From this perspective, Thursday's panic was an overreaction, amplified by the fact that AI stocks had risen so far, so fast. Other factors also played a role: the chipmaker Qualcomm reported disappointing smartphone-chip sales the same day, and its shares fell 9.5 percent. Ipek Ozkardeskaya, a senior analyst at Swissquote Bank, described the moves as a rotation, with money shifting from technology to other sectors and from US markets to non-US ones, rather than a collapse.

Skeptics, however, see deeper cracks. Even before the election, investors were questioning whether the enormous spending on AI would ever generate sufficient returns, especially at a time of high interest rates. Goldman Sachs has estimated that AI-related capital spending could total around $7.6 trillion between 2026 and 2031, across chips, data centres and power supply. Such sums rest on the assumption that projects can be built quickly and relatively cheaply. If regulation lengthens approval times or forces companies to pay more of their own energy costs, the business case for some projects may weaken considerably.

The episode illustrates a broader lesson about markets. Share prices are not only a measure of present profits; they are a forecast of future ones, and forecasts depend on assumptions that may be political as well as technical. For years, the AI trade rested on the belief that the main limit on growth was engineering capacity. Thursday suggested that public consent may be an equally important constraint. Whether the sell-off proves to be a brief stumble or the beginning of a more cautious era, it has made one point clear: even the most advanced technologies must ultimately be built in real places, with the permission of the people who live there.

speak.p: Some people think that new technologies should be developed as quickly as possible, while others believe development should slow down until the risks are better understood. Which view do you agree with? Use specific reasons and examples to support your answer.
speak.hint: Opinion in one sentence → reason 1 + example → reason 2 + example → short wrap-up.

write.p: Professor: Huge data centres are needed to power artificial intelligence, but they use large amounts of electricity and water and can raise local utility bills. Some people argue that local residents should be able to vote to stop new data centres in their area. Others believe such decisions should be made by national governments, because the technology benefits the whole country. Which approach do you think is better, and why? (Mia says: I think local residents should have the final say. They are the ones who live next to these facilities and deal with higher power bills and constant noise. If a project truly benefits the community, the company should be able to convince people to support it. Kevin says: I disagree. If every town can block a data centre, the country will fall behind in an important technology. National governments can see the bigger picture and can require companies to compensate local communities, for example by paying for new power plants.)

articles.title: A Pinch of Prevention: Could Swapping Salt Save Millions of Lives?
articles.dek: A simple salt swap could save millions of lives. But should governments decide what goes into our food?
paras: Few ingredients are as ordinary as table salt, yet few have such an outsized effect on human health. Salt is made mostly of sodium chloride, and diets high in sodium are one of the best-established causes of high blood pressure, which in turn raises the risk of heart attacks, strokes and kidney disease. A modelling study published on November 4, 2026, in the journal Nature Health suggests that a surprisingly simple change, replacing ordinary salt with a potassium-enriched alternative, could prevent close to three million deaths worldwide every year.

The logic behind the idea is straightforward. Most people consume too much sodium and too little potassium, and both imbalances push blood pressure upward. Potassium-enriched salt replaces part of the sodium chloride with potassium chloride, so a single product tackles both problems at once. Crucially, it looks, tastes and cooks much like regular salt, which means people do not have to change their habits or give up flavour. In 2025, the World Health Organization endorsed its use as a way to lower blood pressure and reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease, which killed about 19.2 million people worldwide in 2023.

Researchers from The George Institute for Global Health estimated the effects of such a switch across 193 countries. In their most ambitious scenario, in which all salt is replaced, including both the salt people add at home and the salt hidden in processed and restaurant food, about 2.96 million deaths and 10.17 million new cases of cardiovascular and kidney disease would be avoided each year. Even narrower scenarios produced large gains: switching only the salt used at home would prevent an estimated 1.85 million deaths. China, where much of the salt is added during home cooking, would benefit most, with more than one million deaths avoided annually.

The study builds on earlier evidence. In a large trial published in 2021, researchers followed about 21,000 people in 600 villages in rural China, all of whom had a history of stroke or were older adults with high blood pressure. Those who used the salt substitute had a 14 percent lower risk of stroke and 12 percent fewer premature deaths than those who kept using regular salt. The new study takes results like these and projects them onto the entire world, which is both its strength and its limitation.

That limitation is worth examining. A modelling study does not observe what actually happens; it calculates what would happen if certain assumptions hold. The headline figures assume that people switch completely and that the benefits seen in trials apply equally in very different populations. In reality, adoption is rarely complete, and diets vary enormously. In Europe and North America, for example, more than 70 percent of salt intake comes from processed and restaurant foods rather than from the salt shaker. In those regions, the authors acknowledge, meaningful progress depends less on individual shoppers than on whether food manufacturers agree to change their recipes. Producing enough potassium chloride to meet a sudden surge in demand would also be a challenge.

Safety is another concern. For most people, extra potassium is harmless or even beneficial, but in patients with advanced kidney disease, the body may struggle to remove it, leading to a dangerous condition called hyperkalaemia. The study concluded that even in this group the benefits outweighed the risks, but the researchers stress that people with serious kidney problems, or those taking medicines that raise potassium levels, need precautions such as clear product labelling, patient education and medical supervision.

These caveats raise a broader policy question. Should governments simply encourage people to choose the healthier salt, or should they require manufacturers to use it? Supporters of stronger action argue that individual choice has limited power when most salt is hidden in packaged foods, and that a change built into the food supply would protect people without asking them to do anything. Critics worry about the cost to industry, the risks to a vulnerable minority, and the principle of governments altering what people eat without their explicit consent.

Bruce Neal, a senior researcher at The George Institute, has argued that the approach offers greater potential at much lower cost than many drug-based treatments. Whether that potential is realised will depend less on laboratory science than on politics, economics and public trust. The humble salt shaker, it turns out, is a surprisingly good place to begin a debate about how societies balance collective health against individual freedom.

write.p: Professor: A new study suggests that replacing ordinary salt with a potassium-enriched alternative could prevent millions of deaths each year. Some people believe governments should make this switch compulsory for food manufacturers. Others think governments should only provide information and let people decide for themselves. Which approach do you support, and why? (Daniel says: I support making it compulsory. Most of the salt we eat is already inside packaged food, so individuals don't really have a choice anyway. A rule for manufacturers would protect everyone, including people who never read nutrition labels. Sophie says: I prefer the information approach. A small group of people, such as patients with kidney disease, could be harmed by extra potassium. If the change is compulsory, it becomes much harder for them to avoid it. People should be trusted to make their own decisions.)

articles.title: The Sound of Trouble: How Human Noise Is Reshaping the Animal World
articles.dek: Noise changes 80 percent of the animal species studied. Should quiet be protected like forests and rivers?
paras: When people think about pollution, they usually picture something visible: smoke rising from factories, plastic floating in the ocean, oil coating a beach. Noise rarely makes the list. Yet a major study published on November 5, 2026, in the journal Science suggests that the sounds of human activity, from traffic and shipping to construction and aircraft, may be one of the most widespread and underestimated threats facing wildlife.

The research was carried out by Hansjoerg Kunc and Rouven Schmidt, behavioural ecologists at Queen's University Belfast. Rather than running a single new experiment, they performed a meta-analysis, a statistical method that combines the results of many earlier studies to reveal patterns that no single study could detect. They gathered data from 214 experimental studies covering 177 species of animals on land and in water, across six continents. Because closely related species often respond in similar ways simply because they share common ancestors, the researchers also adjusted their analysis for evolutionary relationships.

The headline result is striking. Noise altered at least one physiological, developmental or behavioural trait in about 80 percent of the species examined. The effects were not limited to minor changes in behaviour. In house sparrows, for instance, chicks exposed to noise, including traffic noise, showed early signs of accelerated ageing and weaker defences against predators. Young Atlantic cod exposed to noise as larvae grew more slowly and were more likely to die. Researchers even recorded measurable changes in gene activity. On average, there were about 37 percent fewer animals in noisy areas than in quiet ones.

Noise also reshapes relationships between species. Many predators rely on sound to locate prey, so a noisy environment makes hunting harder. Across the studies, predators exposed to noise invested about 2.5 times as much effort in hunting yet caught roughly a quarter less prey. Meanwhile, prey animals often became more vigilant, spending time watching for danger that might otherwise be spent feeding. Not every species suffers equally, however. Bats, which hunt by echolocation, are clear losers in noisy settings, whereas some moths that bats feed on may actually benefit, since their main enemy becomes less effective. Noise, in other words, does not simply harm nature; it rearranges it, producing winners as well as losers.

Why has this problem received so little attention? Part of the answer is that sound leaves no visible trace. A polluted river can be photographed, but a noisy forest looks exactly like a quiet one. Noise is also difficult to regulate because its sources are so diverse and so closely tied to economic activity. Roads, ports, airports and energy projects all generate sound, and each brings real benefits to people. Reducing noise can therefore mean slowing ships, rerouting flights or redesigning machinery, all measures that cost money and may face resistance.

The researchers argue that conservation policy should treat soundscapes, the total acoustic environment of a place, as seriously as physical habitats. Kunc has called for low-noise zones that would give animals a genuine acoustic refuge. Such ideas are not without precedent: some ports have asked ships to slow down in areas used by whales, partly to reduce underwater noise, and some cities have laid quieter road surfaces. Supporters point out that many of these measures also benefit people, since long-term exposure to noise has been linked to stress and heart disease in humans.

Others urge caution in interpreting the findings. Many of the studies included were carried out under experimental conditions, which may not perfectly reflect how animals respond in the wild, where they can sometimes move away or gradually adjust. Moreover, strictly protecting quiet areas could limit development in regions that genuinely need new roads or energy supplies. Balancing these interests will require careful, case-by-case decisions rather than blanket rules.

Still, the study shifts the burden of proof. It is no longer reasonable to assume that noise is merely an annoyance for wildlife. As human activity spreads into even the most remote landscapes, the question is not whether we are changing the sound of the planet, but whether we are willing to listen to what that change is costing.

keySentences.text: Yet a major study published on November 5, 2026, in the journal Science suggests that the sounds of human activity, from traffic and shipping to construction and aircraft, may be one of the most widespread and underestimated threats facing wildlife.
keySentences.note: "Yet" contrasts noise with visible pollution and introduces the thesis.

keySentences.text: Noise altered at least one physiological, developmental or behavioural trait in about 80 percent of the species examined.
keySentences.note: The central finding. Number questions often paraphrase "about 80 percent" as "four in five".

keySentences.text: Noise, in other words, does not simply harm nature; it rearranges it, producing winners as well as losers.
keySentences.note: "In other words" signals a restatement: the bat-and-moth example supports this idea.

keySentences.text: Part of the answer is that sound leaves no visible trace.
keySentences.note: Explains why the problem was ignored; useful for inference questions about attention and regulation.

keySentences.text: The researchers argue that conservation policy should treat soundscapes, the total acoustic environment of a place, as seriously as physical habitats.
keySentences.note: The researchers' recommendation; note the definition given in apposition.

keySentences.text: Others urge caution in interpreting the findings.
keySentences.note: Introduces the counter-argument. TOEFL often asks how a paragraph relates to the one before it.

questions.q: The word “invested” in paragraph 4 is closest in meaning to
opts: put money into
gave authority to
surrounded
devoted
questions.why: "Invested effort in" means devoted or spent effort on something.
questions.evidence: predators exposed to noise invested about 2.5 times as much effort in hunting
optWhy: Another meaning of the word: "invest" usually means put money in, but the object here is effort.
Another meaning of the word: "invest someone with power" means give authority, a different structure.
Another meaning of the word: an old military sense means surround, which does not fit.
Correct. Predators devoted more effort to hunting.

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, why did the researchers adjust their analysis for evolutionary relationships?
opts: Because they wanted to compare animals living on different continents
Because related species may react similarly just because they share ancestors
Because earlier studies had focused only on species that live in water
Because they needed to identify which species were closest to extinction
questions.why: Related species may react alike only because they share ancestors, so the analysis was adjusted for this.
questions.evidence: Because closely related species often respond in similar ways simply because they share common ancestors, the researchers also adjusted their analysis for evolutionary relationships.
optWhy: True but not the question: six continents describes the study's range, not the reason for the adjustment.
Correct. Paraphrases "share common ancestors".
Contradicts the passage: the study covered animals on land and in water, and earlier studies are not described this way.
Not mentioned: the passage says nothing about ranking species by extinction risk.

questions.q: According to paragraph 3, all of the following are effects of noise on animals EXCEPT:
opts: signs of faster ageing in young birds
slower growth and higher death rates in young fish
louder and more frequent calls in most bird species
lower numbers of animals in noisy areas
questions.why: Paragraph 3 does not mention louder or more frequent bird calls.
questions.evidence: In house sparrows, for instance, chicks exposed to noise, including traffic noise, showed early signs of accelerated ageing and weaker defences against predators.
optWhy: Stated: house sparrow chicks showed accelerated ageing.
Stated: young cod grew more slowly and were more likely to die.
Correct. Not mentioned in paragraph 3.
Stated: there were about 37 percent fewer animals in noisy areas.

questions.q: Why does the author mention bats and moths in paragraph 4?
opts: To illustrate that noise can help some species while harming others
To show that insects are generally more sensitive to noise than mammals
To explain how echolocation was first discovered by scientists
To argue that bats should be protected more than any other species
questions.why: Bats lose while some moths may benefit, which shows that noise creates winners as well as losers.
questions.evidence: Not every species suffers equally, however.
optWhy: Correct. The example supports "Not every species suffers equally."
Too extreme: one example cannot show insects are generally more sensitive, and the moths may benefit.
Not mentioned: the passage does not explain how echolocation was discovered.
Not mentioned: the author does not say bats deserve more protection than other species.

questions.q: What can be inferred from paragraph 5 about noise pollution?
opts: It is less harmful than water pollution because it cannot be seen.
It can be easily solved by banning traffic near forests.
Most people do not notice noise in their daily lives.
Efforts to reduce it are likely to involve trade-offs with economic interests.
questions.why: Noise sources are tied to useful economic activity, and cutting noise costs money and meets resistance, so trade-offs are likely.
questions.evidence: Reducing noise can therefore mean slowing ships, rerouting flights or redesigning machinery, all measures that cost money and may face resistance.
optWhy: Cause reversed: being invisible explains why noise is ignored, not that it is less harmful.
Too extreme: the paragraph stresses that noise is hard to regulate and never mentions banning traffic.
Not mentioned: the paragraph is about attention and regulation, not whether people notice noise.
Correct. Reducing noise involves costs and resistance from economic interests.

questions.q: Which of the sentences below best expresses the essential information in the highlighted sentence in paragraph 8? Incorrect choices change the meaning in important ways or leave out essential information.
opts: Since humans are clearly changing the planet's sounds, the real issue is whether we will face the costs.
Scientists remain uncertain whether the spread of human activity is really changing the sound of remote landscapes.
Human activity should be prevented from spreading into remote landscapes because it makes the planet far too noisy.
People living in remote landscapes are unwilling to listen to scientists who study the sounds of the planet.
questions.why: Humans are clearly changing the planet's sound; the real question is whether we will face the costs.
questions.evidence: the question is not whether we are changing the sound of the planet, but whether we are willing to listen to what that change is costing.
optWhy: Correct. Keeps the "not whether A but whether B" logic.
Cause reversed: the sentence treats the change as a fact, not a doubt.
Not mentioned: the sentence does not call for stopping human activity.
Detail swapped: "listen" is a metaphor for facing the costs, not listening to scientists.
questions.highlight: As human activity spreads into even the most remote landscapes, the question is not whether we are changing the sound of the planet, but whether we are willing to listen to what that change is costing.

speak.p: Some people say the most effective way to protect the environment is through government regulation. Others believe individual actions, such as changing daily habits, are more effective. Which do you think is more important, and why?
speak.hint: Pick a side → one reason with an example from the article → one reason from your own life → wrap-up.

write.p: Professor: A major new study shows that human-made noise harms about 80 percent of the animal species studied. Some people argue that governments should set strict limits on noise from roads, ships and airports, even if this increases costs. Others think that noise is a minor problem compared with issues like habitat loss and climate change, so limited resources should go elsewhere. What is your view? (Lucas says: I think strict limits are necessary. Noise affects so many species, and it also harms human health. Quieter engines and road surfaces would help both people and wildlife, so the extra cost is worth it. Emma says: I see the problem, but I think habitat loss is a far bigger threat. If an animal has no forest to live in, it doesn't matter how quiet the area is. Governments should focus their money on protecting land first.)

Give a reason supported by the article.
